prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. Road User Type

- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

This was driven home by observations of the homeless living on the streets, and how they are seen as “little disturbances”. For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Collectively, these responses reflect a strong consensus that redesigning infrastructure is essential for creating a safer and fairer transport system that can effectively integrate CAVs. 3.5.3. Inclusivity and accessibility Codes such as “inclusive design,” “accessible vehicles,” and “no burden on VRUs” reflected participants’ concerns about marginalised groups, particularly people with disabilities, the elderly, and those without access to wearable technology. Concerns around inclusivity and accessibility were prominent, with participants firmly rejecting policies that placed the burden of adaptation on VRUs. Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. One participant voiced their frustration: “Pedestrians should NOT have to wear something so that these cars can see them… If the robot can’t see pedestrians, then it should not be allowed on the road” (NB, 18). Another participant echoed this sentiment: “There is no way you can insist that all people walking around roads must have a smartphone with a specific app or wear hi-vis clothing; that is silly. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road.
